question_text: A 14-year-old girl comes to the physician for exertional leg pain. The pain began last week when she started jogging to lose weight. She is at the 5th percentile for height and 80th percentile for weight. Physical examination shows a broad neck with bilateral excess skin folds that extend to the shoulders, as well as a low-set hairline and ears. There is an increased carrying angle when she fully extends her arms at her sides. Pulses are palpable in all extremities; lower leg pulses are delayed. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?

                    ### Question
                    A 14-year-old girl comes to the physician for exertional leg pain. The pain began last week when she started jogging to lose weight. She is at the 5th percentile for height and 80th percentile for weight. Physical examination shows a broad neck with bilateral excess skin folds that extend to the shoulders, as well as a low-set hairline and ears. There is an increased carrying angle when she fully extends her arms at her sides. Pulses are palpable in all extremities; lower leg pulses are delayed. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Ovarian dysgenesis
opb. Absent uterus
opc. Mitral valve prolapse
opd. Triphalangeal thumb
ope. Horseshoe adrenal gland

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The clinical presentation of the 14-year-old girl, including short stature, broad neck with excess skin folds, increased carrying angle (cubitus valgus), and delayed lower leg pulses, is highly suggestive of Turner syndrome. Turner syndrome is a genetic condition characterized by the partial or complete absence of one X chromosome. A common feature of Turner syndrome is ovarian dysgenesis, leading to primary amenorrhea and infertility. The retrieved evidence path linking symptoms to Turner's syndrome supports this diagnosis. Other options, such as absent uterus, mitral valve prolapse, triphalangeal thumb, and horseshoe adrenal gland, are not typically associated with Turner syndrome. Therefore, the most likely additional finding in this patient is ovarian dysgenesis, consistent with the consensus on Turner syndrome's clinical features.
